Deputy Governor’s Opening Speech at the Launch of the Directors' Remuneration Report 2015
Speaker
: Datuk Nor Shamsiah Mohd Yunus
Venue
: Lanai Kijang, Kuala Lumpur
Delivery Date
:
07 Dec. 2015
Since its inception, the FIDE Forum has played an important role in bringing corporate governance issues to the centre-stage, with the continuing active participation of directors of financial institutions. In 2010, the FIDE Forum commissioned a study titled “Performance Pays” which advocated performance-driven remuneration for non-executive directors in Malaysia. The report to be launched today is another important initiative and valuable resource for boards. It will shed light on board practices on remuneration and contain specific recommendations to further advance efforts to strengthen corporate governance within the financial sector.
The success or failure of any organisation is often attributed to the quality of its corporate governance. In heavily regulated sectors like banking and insurance, the collapse of financial institutions especially major global players invariably invites greater public scrutiny and the tightening of rules and regulations. This is what we saw in the aftermath of the global financial crisis in 2008. While it is important that the relevant corporate governance standards are further strengthened, this must be reinforced by an honest reflection on gaps that exist in practice and a strong response by those at the very top of the organisation to elevate an institution’s governance practices and arrangements. It is in our collective interests to ensure that corporate governance practices in the financial sector remain sound over time. Regulation alone will not achieve this.
As key public interest entities, financial institutions are expected to lead by example and remain at the forefront in regard to corporate governance practices. At the same time, greater expectations being placed on board members and the growing complexity of the business has increased the challenge of attracting the highly capable talents to join the board of a financial institution. Indeed, some may view that the weight of regulatory expectations and potential personal liability associated with being on the board of a financial institution has outstripped the professional satisfaction gained from such appointments.
So, how can we move forward in resolving these tensions? In answering that question, I thought I would share some perspectives with you on our observations of board practices, drawing largely from our supervisory work.
Rethinking the board’s oversight approach
The first concerns re-thinking the board’s oversight approach. In recent years, regulatory concerns are increasingly dominating the agendas of many boards, both globally and in Malaysia. Regulatory frameworks must of course evolve to reflect not only the changing environment, but also maturing financial institutions and supervisory systems. But directors of financial institutions today would be forgiven, particularly in the more recent period following the financial crisis, for feeling overwhelmed by the continuous onslaught of new rules and regulations.
A common reaction by boards has been to view each new obligation imposed on boards in isolation, adding incrementally to an already long and daunting list of “things to do” for the board. This can detract boards from maintaining a strong focus on their primary roles in strategy and monitoring the performance of senior management.
For sure, stronger regulation has resulted in an increased emphasis on the board’s oversight role. This is embedded in the Financial Services Act 2013 which expands and elaborates the duties of the board of a financial institution. The aim of regulation, however, is to ensure that boards implement a strong accountability framework for their institutions, and are actively engaged in the strategic business direction and oversight of risks of the institution. In other words, the board is expected to keep management “honest”, and be able to hold management to account for ensuring that the institution operates in a responsible manner in creating value for its stakeholders. In the case of financial institutions, the stakeholders are clearly not just the shareholders, employees and direct customers, but a much wider community of regulators, market participants and taxpayers that may be on the hook if an institution fails.
Responding to each new regulatory development or emerging issue with a corresponding new or extended compliance and reporting process would achieve little more than longer board meetings and more voluminous board papers. It is therefore incumbent on boards to develop and maintain a cohesive approach to oversight. New and changing demands on the board should lead the board to keep under constant review how it will optimally function and the board dynamics. They should not merely increase board activity. In the area of risk, the Bank expects boards to devote time and rigour to deliberate and articulate a clear risk appetite framework which acts as a strong anchor for risk-taking across the organisation. But the board should direct and hold management to account for the operational aspects of the framework, including its effective implementation and promoting a sound risk culture. Only then can the board focus, as it should, on enterprise risks; sustain an active dialogue on emerging issues; and spend time understanding the impact of external conditions on the institution’s strategy and internal capacity to adapt and evolve.
This is especially critical in uncertain and difficult times. But more fundamentally, it is needed to energise and keep boards engaged and able to discharge their roles effectively. Done well, boards are likely to identify opportunities to further enhance board performance, including through improvements to board processes.
Ensuring succession preparedness
Effective oversight by the board invariably builds on strong management. This brings me to my second point which relates to the board’s role in ensuring that a strong senior management team is in place and maintained with well-executed succession plans.
Ensuring succession preparedness may well be the single most important role of the board. At a time when performance will depend on successfully delivering carefully crafted business strategies to address the effects of regulatory reform, technology change and market movements, financial institutions can ill afford disruptive transitions, or worse, leadership vacuums. In reality however, leadership changes in the domestic financial industry have often been less than ideal and the Bank has lately further intensified its engagements with financial institutions to change this.
But there is another reason for boards to focus on succession. It is to reduce risks to boards themselves and increase the confidence of boards in performing their role as effective stewards of the institution. A strong management team can significantly alter the risk-reward balance for new talent joining the board. This in turn will strengthen the board’s own succession and substantially improve prospects for the board itself to be rejuvenated.
Promoting a healthy board culture
My final point relates to board culture. It is widely acknowledged that a healthy board culture can be a key driver of board effectiveness. The emphasis on culture in the period since the global financial crisis stems from a recognition that behaviour is shaped by influences that run much deeper than policies, systems and processes which aim to regulate behaviour. This is also true for boards. A boardroom environment that values individual contributions, and that encourages spirited discussions and dissent allows directors to meaningfully shape the outcomes for the organisation. Boards should reflect a wide range of skills and experiences that can be drawn upon to expand perspectives and build collective knowledge, both of which are important ingredients for better decisions.
At the same time, boards will need to make greater progress in areas that tend to be more sensitive, but which can significantly lift board performance. This includes improving the rigour and effectiveness of board evaluations, development and compensation. Keeping boards of financial institutions at the top of their game is not only good for the institution and the broader financial system; it is a valuable opportunity for individuals who are serving on boards to grow professionally.
With more wide-ranging demands, how a financial institution rewards its board and taps into the talent pipeline for directors will be essential. There is no “one-size-fits-all” solution. But at its most basic level, any incentive system for boards must enable a financial institution to attract the specific skill sets and experience it requires on the board. This must also reflect the business and particular challenges that may be faced by an institution, for which the board will be expected to provide leadership.
In FIDE Forum’s 2010 report, expanded further in its latest report, the case is made for “fair and equitable remuneration”, with practical guidance on how to best approach the design of board compensation. Broad-brushed approaches comparing absolute levels of compensation across financial institutions, which are still common in the industry, are shown to be woefully inadequate to reflect the level of time commitment and responsibilities, as well as the opportunity cost for individuals with specialised skills taking up directorships in financial institutions. Importantly, interactions between board compensation, board evaluations and succession plans need to be carefully approached as part of a cohesive system which works together to elevate board performance. In all of this, the independent judgment of the board in setting overall strategy and risk appetite and overseeing senior management performance must always be preserved.
Conclusion
The subject of corporate governance covers a broad canvas. I have chosen this morning to speak briefly on re-thinking the board’s oversight approach, ensuring succession preparedness and promoting a healthy board culture because I believe these are particularly relevant to the challenge of ensuring sustainable high performing boards going forward. The Bank is greatly encouraged by the work of FIDE Forum and Iclif which has had, and continues to have, an important impact in building stronger boards in our financial institutions, and leading the way in board education and development. I would encourage financial institutions to participate in and support the activities of FIDE Forum which provide unparalleled opportunities for directors of financial institutions in Malaysia to interact on common issues with one another and the world’s leading experts in the field of governance.
I am confident that the recommendations set out in the Directors’ Remuneration Report 2015 will further deepen our collective body of knowledge on how we can build highly effective boards. Drawing upon these insights, I hope to see financial institutions coming together and proactively prioritising initiatives and resources to better manage the talent pool for directors.
With that, it is my great pleasure to launch FIDE Forum’s Directors’ Remuneration Report 2015.
title: Deputy Governor’s Opening Speech at the Launch of the Directors' Remuneration Report 2015

Deputy Governor's Keynote Address at the 10th Anniversary Dinner of IIUM Institute Islamic Banking and Finance -"Islamic Finance and Education, Thinking Beyond"
Speaker
: Muhammad bin Ibrahim, FCB
Venue
: IIUM Gombak Campus
Delivery Date
:
04 Dec. 2015
The 10th Anniversary Dinner of IIUM Institute of Islamic Banking and Finance (IiBF) is a significant milestone. As an alumni, I am proud that the institute has made great strides in developing and producing the required talent for the Islamic finance industry. Over the years, the IiBF has produced increasing number of Islamic finance graduates and we should take pride that a total of 14 PhD students have graduated this year, the highest number of graduates so far. We should aspire for our alumni and IiBF graduates to become captains and leaders of the industry. It is only this outcome that the institute should benchmark itself in measuring its success.
While the celebration of success is well deserved for our Institute, as it in itself an important element to motivate and inspire continuous achievements, I believe at the same time, it would be meaningful if we reflect on our achievements and assess the extent of our success in upholding the true values of Islamic finance. While we acknowledge the steady growth and commendable milestones achieved in the industry over the last three decades, I thought we should ask ourselves, where does Islamic finance really stand today? Have we truly embraced the Islamic values embedded in Shariah and become a role model of ethics? Has Islamic finance been really innovative? Or simply adaptive? How successful are we in bringing about the required changes in the society that could contribute towards the betterment of the lives of the general public?
Let us go back to the thirteenth century where Islamic civilisation was the epitome of social, economic and learning progress. The Muslim empire during the golden age of Islam has given birth to prominent Islamic scholars whom have pioneered many innovations and breakthroughs. These outstanding inventions in the Muslim world have paved the way for global civilisations, so much so, that Islam became torch bearers of various disciplines including science, mathematics and philosophy. The flourish of Islam was attributable to the Muslims’ endless pursuit of knowledge, their openness to learn from earlier civilisations and their stance against any forms of inequality or prejudices.
Now, the state of the Muslims throughout the world is in disarray. Poverty, illiteracy and suppression of civil society are a few of the many challenges faced by the ummah. While the world environment and civilisation has changed and many people and countries have transformed and progress through the centuries, the Muslims conditions are worse than before.
We are embroiled in polemics, endless disagreements, civil wars and strifes. We forgot about past success that could inspire us to take new leads to improve the conditions of the ummah. We are, it seems, to be forever in a state of quagmire. Many Muslims like to speak about the past but we should not speak of the old glory days of Islam and do nothing about it and continue to fall back and rely on the great inventions of the past. We ought not hold on to practices and views of yesteryears that were suitable for a foregone era but instead make brave and bold
ijtihad
that can position our religion at the cutting edge of technology, science and philosophy. It is most unfortunate to observe that most Muslim countries today are experiencing poor social and economic growth and are being left far behind compared to other nations. Why is this happening? Is it the religion? Is it the way it is being taught or practised?
I believe that the sad reality of the current Muslim world is a reflection of the state of individuals in our society today. Our Ummah now is weak and at a low ebb. We lack the tolerance to opinions that contradict ours and we are too reckless in rejecting differing views. We are too quick to criticise and too hurried in passing judgement. We amplify pettiness and trivialise substantive matters. Our tendency to remain simplistic makes us lax in thinking and prevent deep thinking in coming up with solutions. These negative traits are ingrained characteristics that have been holding back the Muslim community from making progress. If we want to reawaken the Ummah, we need to embark upon a paradigm shift in our thinking, in our philosophy, in our technology, in our behaviour.
Stop dwelling in issues of no significance and giving frivolous opinions on irrelevant matters. Start opening our minds by taking advantage of lessons derived from other great civilisations. As advocated by the Quran,
“Allah will not change the condition of a people until they change what is in themselves”
(Surah Ar-ra’d, verse 11).
The same holds true for Islamic finance. What has brought us this far would not guarantee success over the future. History is rife with many examples of ideas, concepts and industries that were conceived or invented in one place but were perfected elsewhere and hence found a new thriving home far from those who had originally invented it. If we are not alert and maintain the disposition to preserve or conserve what has been established and traditional; these tendencies to limit change would become the norm. This is dangerous as parochial thinking and dogmatism would be developed and bring development of Islamic finance to a standstill, preventing the industry to progress to a new level of excellence.
Islamic finance has grabbed the attention of many, including multinational financial institutions in London, Paris, New York and Hong Kong. The IMF and the World Bank have allocated resources in the understanding and conducting of surveillance in the growth and application of Islamic finance. If we do not innovate and expand the lead we have now, we may see a shift of activities and dynamism of Islamic finance to somewhere else. And the centre of gravity for what has always been our claim to fame will drift away from us.
History has shown that the Islamic civilisation has only grown when conventional and mainstream thinking were challenged and the propositions of fresh ideas that were built upon research, science and logic were propounded. To ensure dynamism and progress, we should begin by throwing away disruptive habits of amplifying differences and staying away from being too rigid and too narrow mindedness. Instead, more focus should be directed to the commonalities and the need for our minds to remain open and expansive. We ought to stop our damaging behavior on amplifying differences that leads to disunity and instead focus on common good that bring us together.
In the context of Malaysia, Islamic finance presents vast opportunity for greater innovation to take place. Given our three decades of journey in developing Islamic finance, we should be confident enough to show leadership as our tireless efforts have brought the industry to the fore, increasingly making Islamic finance mainstream. But the skills and conceptual thinking that have pioneered our progress since the 1980s have most likely served its purpose. In forging ahead, we require a new way of thinking that is totally divorced from the mainstream views of today. Allow me to quote a hadith that may motivate us to undertake this calling;
“He who introduced some good practice in Islamic which was followed after him (by people), he would be assured of reward like one who followed it”.
(Narrated by Sahih Muslim)
From that perspective, the future will greatly reward people of courage whom are bold enough to envision outcomes that are exclusive from the contemporary thinking. Tonight, I would like to raise some viewpoints relating to a design thinking in nurturing talent in the Islamic finance industry which I hope would spark reassessment in talent development.
I will start with the first verse that was sent down to the Prophet Muhammad s.a.w, that is Iqra (read). Are Muslims nowadays among the great readers? As the first revelation, this verse marks the importance of reading in the pursuit of knowledge. In Islam, people of knowledge are held in high esteem. But without useful knowledge, making progress is impossible. Students of Islamic finance are therefore expected to have the thirst and hunger for knowledge and strive to be great readers. Equally important is the mastery of knowledge in diverse fields of disciplines to ensure comprehensive understanding of relevant subjects to make Islamic finance complete.
In the ‘Lost Enlightenment’ by Frederick Starr, the glory of Central Asia as a leading Islamic civilisation during the years between 800 to 1200 was manifested by its leadership in the development of trade and economy; its cities that were renowned for their sheer size and sophistication; the refinement of its art and more importantly its pioneering knowledge in various fields. The Muslims in Central Asians made significant breakthroughs in mathematics, astronomy, geology, medicine, chemistry, social sciences, philosophy, theology and music, just to name a few.
They were ahead of their time and could use unprecedented precision in calculating the earth’s diameter, and authored many books that became important references on European medicine later during the century. Their creativity also shone through their poetic works which are known to be some of the world’s greatest poetries. They even named algebra. It is astonishing that a scholar working in Afghanistan could even prophesize that North and South America would exist, ahead of Columbus by five centuries. It is impressive that such an elite league of polymaths had appeared within a similar era of history. It is of no surprise that their masterpieces could greatly influence the European culture, beginning from the period of St. Thomas Aquinas until the scientific revolution, with similar tremendous impact in India and majority of Asia.
It is in this spirit that our Islamic finance industry therefore needs a new cadre of Islamic finance developers whom are conversant not only in Shariah, but also in other related areas such as legal, economics, mathematics and finance. We need a group of scholars with multidisciplinary backgrounds whom have freed themselves from parochial thinking and straitjacketing. With diversity in knowledge, our talent in Islamic finance will possess an innate ability to mobilise the conceptual thinking propagated by various sects or Mazhabs in different Islamic schools of thought.
Let us take an example from Imam Al Nawawi, one of the distinguished Islamic scholars whose work has benefitted thousands of people. His great desire for learning has driven him to author more than 40 books ranging from hadith, theology and jurisprudence, in his mere 45 years of living. If Imam Al Nawawi could write that many books of everlasting value in such a short period of lifetime, we should be capable of contributing more to the wealth of Islamic finance knowledge especially with greater access to information and technology at the present time. Unfortunately, it is sad to note that in the Islamic finance education today, we are short of basic textbooks that can be used as reference materials. Similarly, great works of yesteryears are not being translated. Books by Al Tabari, the great historian were only translated into English in 2000, more than 1000 years after they were first authored. Most Muslims, not conversant in Arabic, were not able to learn the lessons of history from a direct source. Instead, they have to rely on subsequent scholars for interpretations, views and opinions. This is in stark contrast where books authored by scholars and philosophies of great Muslims thinkers were translated into many languages and formed the basis for the advancement of other civilisations.
Secondly, from great readers, great thinkers are born. Scholars of Islamic finance must not be passive, but active and courageous intellectuals that continuously strive for new breakthrough ideas.
For example, the calibre and prestige of the great scholar, Ibn Taymiyyah, was distinctive not only by the level of knowledge that far excelled from other scholars of his time, but also by his bravery, boldness and nobleness in his teaching, through the issuance of legal verdicts and writing that expanded the boundaries of opinions. Together with his student Ibn Qayyim, they were known to be great thinkers and innovators, with vast knowledge and strong acquaintance with the differences in various mazhabs. During a time of strife and internal chaos, both great scholars were however regarded as heretics and I am sure were isolated and ostracised due to their unorthodox method of thinking and views. It was only many centuries later that their opinions were accepted and became mainstream and formed the basis of many modern Islamic finance contacts.
We need scholars and thinkers of such stature. Ones who possess the courage and the boldness to traverse beyond contemporary issues and accepted norms. For instance, the Malaysian Founding Fathers would not be able to position the country to where it is now without their bold and ‘outrageous’ vision. They have boldly laid the building blocks for future generation and place the country at the forefront of developments. Similarly, we need to be bold and courageous in building the required foundation to lead Islamic finance into the future. The future favors the bold. This adage is true and proven, and reflective of what we had embarked on to chart the growth of Islamic finance in the 1980s.
Thirdly, the talents that will serve the industry must also maintain strong values of ethics and integrity that portray the principled values of Islam. This includes practising mutual respect to differing schools of thought. The differences in the opinions of the various Mazhabs is a blessing to the people as the diverse opinions enable the needs of society to be met. It should not be a cause for division. It should be a course of celebration in the pursuit of intellectual diversity. Hence, the students of Islamic finance must appreciate the intellectual differences and value the flexibility within the variation of views. Nevertheless, it is important to note that acquiring profound understanding on the diversity of opinions is not the endpoint. The criticality is in the application of the diversity. As important is the determination to search for practical and universal solutions and take advantage of common grounds in dealing with these differences.
The ethical characters built through the Islamic value system must be translated and complemented with technical competency and supported by scientific practices. In adapting to the fast-paced developments in the world today, we need to supplement good moral judgement with practical and systematic approach that makes use of various theories and modelling. This is to prepare our talent in making inclusive decisions that are also based on quantitative valuation, on top of qualitative assessment. Embedding modern tools and techniques into the teaching of Islamic finance should help towards meeting this objective.
In imparting these desired traits among the students of Islamic finance, the academia has a big role in setting the right intellectual climate to nurture visionary scholars. Ahead of admitting students, the universities that teach Islamic finance should first shift their mindset when measuring their key success indicators. The measure of effectiveness in an academia should not end at the point of students’ graduation but should extend beyond that mark to include students’ employability, their ability to contribute to practical and innovative solutions to the industry, and their impact to society at large. Therefore, members of the academia should measure their success using indicators beyond the day their students graduated.
As an institution that is among the first to come into contact with our potential talent, universities have the privilege to mould future generations. To attract the brightest minds into the industry, universities should seek for quality talent as early as during student admission. Place high entry requirements for Islamic finance programmes to acquire the best brains for the industry. It is important to impose stronger quality controls at the entry points to capture outstanding talents with the right characteristics who have the potential to produce revolutionary ideas and philosophies. As Islamic finance is a relatively young sector, we need people who possess formidable intellectual capacity as change agents and leaders to move the industry into the millennium.
Rethinking the fundamentals underlining the contemporary curriculum would be the catalyst for development of future Islamic finance education. With the aim to produce outstanding and multi-skilled graduates, the curriculum must strike a balance between academic learning and acquisition of important sets of expertise such as soft skills, agility, and the ability to articulate and sell ideas and strong problem solving ability. There is also a need to upgrade and revamp existing curriculum to equip students with knowledge from diverse disciplines. This will train the students to develop the ability to loop all knowledge and wisdom of previous civilisations and contextualise issues in accordance with the needs of modern times. The comprehension of multiple languages is also useful to understand intimately the success of previous Islamic dominions in different lingos. We want to mould and breed talents in Islamic finance that will become the great thinkers, great philosophers and great pioneers of the future. With these desired qualities ingrained in the curriculum structure, we will get to produce versatile and thinking talents that are highly sought after not only by the Islamic finance industry but by other fields as well. When it comes to quality, we need the IIUM graduates to be self-evident.
As we aspire to be the global leaders, universities of Islamic finance should also continuously improve their learning pedagogy that is cutting-edge and innovative.
Take the example from Harvard Business School that adopts case study methods of learning to produce effective decision makers recognised by the market. MIT, on the other hand, embraces action learning to provide empirical understanding through real life business experiences. In shaping the best talent for Islamic finance, we must develop teaching methodology and strategies that are able to groom our students holistically. Our teaching methodologies must be diverse and current. We must design an approach that transforms the education experiences of our students into the springboard for lifelong learning.
Lastly, we need to professionalise the industry to raise the calibre of Islamic finance talent. Through increased professionalism and ethics, we can promote talents that will preserve the integrity and sanctity of the Islamic finance profession. IIUM can start this journey by adopting the professional standards advocated by the Chartered Institute of Islamic Finance Professionals when developing the curriculum of its Islamic finance programmes in the future. With the necessary accreditation by the Finance Accreditation Agency (FAA), the faculty can elevate the stature of its courses to form part of the students’ professional developments. Ultimately, the adoption of such standards will add to the prestige of this university as it reflects contemporary standards of the industries and in time attract more talented students to take Islamic finance as a vocation.
It is our responsibility as a collective to have the vision and courage to step our game to another level in our endeavor to build talent for the Islamic finance industry. We have a call to answer, and we must not be afraid to fully liberate our thinking and silos and break new grounds. The exceptional Islamic scholars in the past have shown us the way and they have well-exemplified the path we should embark on. It is only with guts, the heart and the burning desire and passion that we can create original ideas and undertake radical changes that would bring about greater transformation in our industry.
Islamic finance should be the leader, not a mere follower, not an adapter.
Islamic finance should be at the cutting edge, not conventional, not mainstream. Islamic finance should be the trailblazer, not a laggard or a straggler.
It is time for us to mould Islamic finance in a totally different light.
title: Deputy Governor's Keynote Address at the 10th Anniversary Dinner of IIUM Institute Islamic Banking and Finance -"Islamic Finance and Education, Thinking Beyond"

Governor's Speech at the Iclif Leadership Energy Asia Summit 2015
Speaker
: Dr. Zeti Akhtar Aziz
Venue
: Sasana Kijang
Delivery Date
:
01 Dec. 2015
Welcome to this year's Leadership Energy Summit Asia organised by our Iclif Leadership and Governance Centre. This is our third summit in the series on leadership energy. The focus on leadership energy reflects its importance in today's leadership. The contemporary environment we are living in has become increasingly more challenging – characterised by highly destabilising and tumultuous events. Not only are we living in a world that has become highly unpredictable and unstable but a world that is being more frequently subject to extreme conditions in which we are tested to the limit. How do we survive against the odds manifested in this environment? It is all about having the ability to endure and prevail. It is also about being able to succeed and thrive in such an environment. It is about being resilient. Resilience is key to surviving in this environment.
Today we are privileged to hear and be inspired from the experience of personalities who not only survived against such great odds but who have also achieved great success. Let me take this opportunity to express our gratitude to our distinguished speakers who have come from different parts of the world to share their knowledge and experience on this subject. It is all about their perseverance and resilience and how they have defied all expectations. The issue before us is the source of their energy to persevere and their courage to stay the course when it all appears to be hopeless.
In the business of central banking we are increasingly being confronted by such extreme conditions. Building resilience is therefore key. I have described central banking as being an unfinished business because there are always new challenges on the horizon, endless demands emerging from an ever changing and more complex environment and great expectations that the Central Bank will provide the solutions to resolve the financial and economic problems that confront us. The Central Bank is also at the forefront in the management of any financial and economic crisis – a phenomenon that continues to plague the world with increasing frequency.
The Central Bank can be described as a high impact organisation. Its decisions or indecisions, its action or inaction will have major and far reaching repercussions and consequences on the economic well being of the public at large and the entire spectrum of businesses. The responsibility and accountability is therefore immense. Our business is about bringing value and benefits to our citizens. In an environment of greater transparency and enhanced communication there is also greater awareness of the prevailing circumstances. This has produced higher expectations for the delivery of results. Energy is derived from this very sense of meaning of what responsibility brings. It is the drive to making the difference to the economic well being of our citizens.
Fiercely knowing this responsibility and accountability is the very source of the intense energy necessary to preform the function of central banking. Knowing the high costs that destabilising developments can have on the people and businesses and its potential damage to the nation is a major prompt of the perseverance to press on, to survive and to succeed. Often we need to just confront the realities and produce a solution when it seems hopeless. Courage is also needed to stay the course. Knowing the stakes are high, knowing that you are being counted upon spurs the unwavering determination.
From my experience as a lifelong career central banker, such extreme conditions that test us to the limit have become increasingly frequent. While there have been many great successes that have been achieved, there have also been those moments that have been most trying and devastating. During such times, developments set you back to a much worse situation than your original position. Those times have arisen from external shocks that are beyond our control, from ambitious agendas that have been met with violent resistance and domestic stress brought on by actions that are in conflict with the Bank's mandate or from political tensions.
The ability to endure, to persevere, to be resilient in the face of such extreme odds is about having a great sense of purpose of what needs to be achieved and the motivation of why it needs to be achieved. The sheer responsibility and the awareness of the accountability that comes with it is the very driver of such perseverance. It is also the fear of failure and knowing the far-reaching and damaging consequences. This is reinforced with the values and the discipline to stay the course to do what is right and to do what is in the interest of the people. The discipline is also important so that the Central Bank is consistent in its behaviour in managing the challenging conditions or in its aspirations to push the frontiers and create great value for the country.
During such times, having great clarity in the vision and on the objective of what is to be achieved becomes paramount. This has to be the starting point if it is to draw on the energies of the entire organisation. Articulating it with great clarity throughout the organisation allows the collective alignment to the goals. This also avoids being diverted by distractions when we are confronted with destabilising times. It is also imperative when we are ambitious with bringing about change and transformation. Knowing clearly the outcomes and the benefits it brings increases the potential of bringing diverse groups within a country and across countries to building the consensus on achieving a common goal.
Another aspect that needs to be mentioned is being paranoid about the worst that could happen. This is sometimes referred to as productive paranoia. Central bankers need to excel as risk managers – knowing what could go wrong and prepare for the worst that is yet to come. In part it involves building the buffers to prepare for the unexpected events before they happen. When I am asked the question about how we are going to manage ‘the lift off' – the normalisation of interest rate by the Federal Reserve in the United States – my response is that it is not what we will do now but what we have done before it happens that will see us through this period. It is not only the buffers that have been built but also the capability that has been developed that will better allow us to intermediate and thus absorb the shock. This will enable us to withstand the volatile financial flows that are already occurring in anticipation of this eventuality.
Sometimes there are also Black Swan events. These are defined as those developments that have a low probability of happening and that is difficult to predict and anticipate. Being paranoid and building the resilience against such shocks will contain its damaging effects. Therefore continuous rigour needs to be applied all the time, during the good times and the challenging times. Vigilance, detecting developments that could signal danger, early recognition of risks are all important. Also knowing how your risk profile changes over time will avoid one being taken by surprise.
Central banking is therefore not for the faint of heart. It not only demands the high levels of energy – not just the physical energy, but that of the emotional, spiritual and the mind. When tested to the limit, it is from these sources of energy from which the strength is derived. Investing in these sources of energy will avoid its depletion. Energy should not be taken for granted. Then there is the courage that is needed. It is derived from your convictions and values that you hold, reinforced by your sense of purpose and what motivates you.
At the Leadership Energy Summit Asia in 2014, I spoke of having the ability to generate and ride on the positive cycle of leadership energy. In mobilising energies in the organisation to be aligned to achieving an outcome, it generates a second round of energy burst from others in the organisation. The continuous positive energy loop provides continuous motivation and momentum in a two way direction and intensifies energy in the organisation. It is a mutually reinforcing phenomenon that I have experienced in the Bank time and again.
Let me conclude my remarks. The demands on leadership is immense. In the current international and domestic environment, it also requires leadership energy that is sustainable. This Leadership Energy Summit will hear from the experience of successful individuals on the source of their energy in generating outcomes and results that have made a difference. We will also learn about other sources of energy from which we can tap on and strengthen. This is the challenge of the new generation of leaders if they will truly be able to make lasting and meaningful changes in their environment.
On this note, let me wish you a highly energised Summit.
title: Governor's Speech at the Iclif Leadership Energy Asia Summit 2015

Deputy Governor’s Officiating Address at the Launch of Greenback 2.0 Project
Speaker
: Muhammad bin Ibrahim, FCB
Venue
: Johor Bahru
Delivery Date
:
29 Nov. 2015
Bagi pihak Bank Negara Malaysia, saya ingin merakamkan penghargaan kepada semua tetamu yang hadir di majlis pelancaran Greenback 2.0 di Bandaraya yang bersejarah, Johor Bahru. Hari ini, kita bersama-sama menyaksikan satu lagi tonggak bersejarah dalam pembangunan industri pengiriman wang di Malaysia. Dalam tempoh masa sedekad, landskap industri ini telah mengalami perkembangan yang pesat hasil teknologi, liberalisasi dalam dasar pengawalan serta perubahan dalam permintaan pelanggan.
Peranan penting industri pengiriman wang terhadap pembangunan insan dan komuniti serta perkembangan ekonomi tidak dapat dinafikan. Perangkaan Bank Dunia telah menunjukkan bahawa pada tahun 2014, sejumlah USD435 bilion wang telah dikirim oleh pekerja migran ke negara asal masing-masing. Dana yang dikirimkan ini adalah sumber penting dalam membasmi kemiskinan dan meningkatkan lagi kualiti hidup jutaan keluarga migran terutamanya di negara-negara kurang membangun.
Disamping itu, perkembangan yang pesat dalam ekonomi merentasi sempadan telah menyebabkan permintaan yang tinggi terhadap perkhidmatan pengiriman wang serta penyelesaian perdagangan yang lebih efisen dan kompetitif.
Projek Greenback 2.0 merupakan satu lagi inisiatif untuk merealisasikan potensi industri pengiriman wang sebagai wahana penting dalam agenda pembangunan insan dan komuniti serta pembangunan ekonomi. Dua matlamat utama projek ini adalah untuk menggalakkan penggunaan perkhidmatan pengiriman wang menerusi saluran yang formal dan memastikan perkhidmatan kiriman wang yang sentiasa kompetitif, efisen dan inklusif.
Malaysia merupakan negara pertama di rantau Asia Pasifik yang menyertai projek ini menerusi kerjasama dengan pihak Bank Dunia. Hasil penelitian pelbagai faktor, Bandaraya Johor Bahru telah dipilih sebagai
"Champion City"
bagi projek Greenback Malaysia yang mensasarkan dua kumpulan sasaran iaitu migran dan industri kecil dan sederhana. Kami berkeyakinan penuh bahawa Bandaraya Johor Bahru boleh menjadi tapak uji atau
"testbed"
yang baik bagi menilai keberkesanan strategi berasaskan pendidikan dan diterajui oleh teknologi dan inovasi yang dilakarkan di bawah projek ini. Kami merancangkan seterusnya yang inisiatif ini, akan diperluaskan ke seluruh negara.
The activities under the Greenback initiative will focus on two specific outcomes
First, promoting a more cost effective remittance services; and
Second, empowering customers to make informed decisions.
Towards a more cost effective remittance services
On the first outcome, the World Bank has set a target to reduce remittance costs to not more than 5% by 2015, while the United Nations has targeted a reduction in the average remittance cost to 3% by 2030. It is estimated that lowering average remittance costs by at least 3 per cent can provide huge savings of over USD20 billion annually for migrants and their families. For those who are sending money home to developing countries, this brings significant social and economic benefits to the families of the migrant workers. Similarly, lower remittance costs will also reduce the cost of transactions for businesses.
In Malaysia, the cost of remittance to the major corridors is still considered on the higher side, estimated to be between 4% to 7% using non-bank remittance providers, and 6% to 9% for banks. We aim to work with the industry to further reduce the remittance cost by at least 2% and 4% through both these channels respectively. This can be achieved with innovative business models, and the smart use of technology with the right people to drive business and process efficiencies. Financial technology, or Fintech, is already making a significant impact in the remittance and payment landscape in more developed economies and eliminated much of the hidden remittance costs.
Leveraging on similar technologies can open up tremendous opportunities for banks and non-banks in Malaysia to penetrate new remittance channels, including mobile remittance, in our effort to enhance accessibility, and reduce costs. Currently, the market share for mobile remittance remains very low at less than 5%. With mobile phone penetration of 144.8%, the scope for expanding this share is enormous, especially among the migrant community.
Empowering customers to make informed decisions
The second important outcome of our initiatives under the Greenback project is empowering customers to make informed decisions. This is also a key part of the Bank's broader outreach program to consumers on financial issues. Some remittances by migrants and businesses are still flowing through informal or illegal channels. Many are still unaware of the risks of using illegal channels and as a result, have lost hard earned monies that can never be recovered. For some families, this can make the difference on decision whether to place a child through school, or being able to support a family member in need of medical attention, or being able to meet financial commitments to stay or expand their business.
Bank Negara Malaysia is committed to increasing the use of formal channels for remittances. We shall continue to take strong actions against illegal operators. Any person who is associated with illegal operators in blatant disregard for the regulations will not be permitted to participate in the industry. But enforcement alone is not sufficient. Consumer education and awareness are important as well. On this issue, we all have a role to play.
The industry players, the respective embassies, business and migrant associations as well as employers should reach out and intensify awareness and education programs on the availability of formal remittance services. With the intensification of enforcement actions by the Bank, it is important for customers to also be aware that aside from losses resulting from fraud, they may also suffer financial losses if they use unauthorized channels when actions are taken against the illegal operators.
Embracing technology and innovation such as the "Pick Remit" mobile application in the Greenback 2.0 project is a tested and proven method in empowering customers with the information to make a conscious remittance choice. Today's launch of the "Pick Remit" mobile application will further enhance transparency and empower customers to make smart remittance choices. This will not only enhance the protection of consumers by directing them to use the services of licensed remittance service providers, but also provide useful information to help consumers choose between remittance services and providers. This in turn, will promote competition and improve the quality and cost of remittance services.
Conclusion
The Greenback initiative aims to work for all of us. I am greatly encouraged by the support and commitment of our strategic partners, the Johor Bharu City Council and the World Bank on this important effort. The industry players and associations gathered here today are also proof of their commitment to make this initiative a success.
For Bank Negara Malaysia, this initiative represents part of a broader agenda to reap the full developmental benefits of remittance services for individuals and businesses that use their services. We are fully committed to supporting the activities under this project to achieve a competitive, convenient and inclusive remittance services.
Dengan lafaz Bismillahirrahmanirrahim, saya berbesar hati untuk merasmikan projek Greenback 2.0 Bandaraya Johor Bahru dan aplikasi mobil, "
Pick Remit".
title: Deputy Governor’s Officiating Address at the Launch of Greenback 2.0 Project

Deputy Governor's Speech at the Launch of "Art of ASEAN: Our Exhibition"
Speaker
: Muhammad bin Ibrahim, FCB
Venue
: Bank Negara Museum and Art Gallery, Sasana Kijang
Delivery Date
:
26 Nov. 2015
Welcome to "Art of ASEAN: Our Exhibition". I would like to specifically welcome Tan Sri Dato' Ajit Singh, the former Secretary of ASEAN as our guest of honour. The exhibition embodies the very purpose of the existence of ASEAN. This exhibition was envisioned, to bring us together for the cause of collaboration. Similarly with this building, it was designed to be a nexus for thought leadership, to hosts a learning centre with an advanced training facilities for developmental programmes and high level seminars for local and foreign participants, as well as providing an avenue for the exchange of views and experiences amongst central banking and financial community.
Sasana Kijang is also now the proud home to five notable organisations; The SEACEN Centre, a regional learning and research Centre for Central Banks in the region and The International Islamic Financial Services Board (IFSB), an international organisation for the setting of prudential standards for Islamic Finance, the Alliance for Financial Inclusion Permanent Headquarters, a global network of developing countries to advance financial inclusion globally. The World Bank Office and Asian School of Business have also become part of the Sasana Kijang community. This is a reflection of our efforts and commitment in promoting greater understanding and collaboration, in particular, amongst the central bank fraternity. In four years since the opening of the Art Galleries, a total of 19 exhibitions were held in this very building.
Common threads are something more often heard about than actually seen. Within ASEAN, there are some threads that are common and also visible. Just as this exhibition weaves together a diversity of cultures, there is in the region, a heritage textile that does this at a practical level.
This is not a textile exhibition, of course. A glance at the walls will confirm this. What we are looking at are the works of contemporary descendants of those cloths that are perhaps the region's richest heritage, and certainly the artifacts most sought-after by collectors around the world. Heirloom fabrics were, in their day, the most revered expression of Southeast Asian societies. They were a canvas on which creativity could be applied, beautifying the surroundings and proclaiming identity.
There is another type of textile in particular that illustrates different routes to the same end, as well as putting this region of ours on the international art map.
'Ikat' cloths exist in many parts of ASEAN and very few other places. Their individually dyed threads, along with the imagination required to create an image that emerges from those threads, mark them out as something requiring commitment and extreme patience. The 'Ikat' cloths are universally admired. The word 'ikat' is a rare example of a Malay/Javanese word that has travelled the globe and been accepted in the English lexicon. It is derived from the word 'mengikat', meaning to tie together, and this provides a useful metaphor for our exhibition.
It is in this context that when I mentioned 'our' exhibition, it does not refer to Bank Negara Malaysia but the word 'our' is a reference to the ASEAN's motto. "Our People, Our Community, Our Vision". It is about bringing people together, as "Ikat" is about bringing threads together, to create a complete picture out of a seemingly incoherent jumble.
The process of "Ikat" weaving means almost-invisible threads of weft holding everything together while the swerved threads are proudly displayed. An apt description of ASEAN, an organization that binds disparate nations without always being visible to the 600-plus million population.
An exhibition such as this provides a physical expression of the generally unseen collaborative power.
'Art of ASEAN: Our Exhibition' shows how societies have developed amidst the rapid globalization process over the last few decades. They are more attuned to global developments while still retaining their own communities' characteristics. These new canvases come in various shapes and sizes that are not so different from the traditional fabrics of the past. They may not be wearable but they still serve the purpose of making a visual statement. The sculptures and installations at our exhibition are also a continuation of a different regional heritage; one that places emphasis on three dimensions rather than two. Every part of ASEAN has this heritage, whether it is the architectural woodcarvings of Islamic societies or the all-out imagery of deities in Hindu, Buddhist, Christian and tribal communities.
With contemporary art, showcasing the works of individual nations is relatively straightforward. But combining them to provide a forum for all of ASEAN is not. There have been very few attempts made at showing the full range of regional creative output. This is not caused by a lack of enthusiasm; it is more about logistics and language barriers.
Just as financial and economic integration is unfolding within ASEAN, there are signs of art becoming a cohesive force. Artists and galleries are moving more freely across borders, bringing ideas and friendships with them.
It's a paradox that the auction capital of Southeast Asia moved from Singapore to Hong Kong some years ago, but maybe a neutral territory is required.
In Malaysia, we are always glad to be host to regional artists in a building that was built for the task. In addition to the "Sasana" part of the Sasana Kijang name, meaning a meeting place of inquiring minds, we must not forget the "Kijang", an animal believed to be intelligent and agile. Despite folklore attributing the barking deer's arrival in the Malay Peninsula to Arab traders, it is indigenous throughout most of Southeast Asia and not many other places. So 'Kijang' fittingly symbolizes the intelligence and the agility of this Region in managing the many challenges that we face as a community.
Although some ASEAN artists have migrated to other parts of the world, most continue to work in their homelands with occasional exchanges within the region. We are very privileged to host the collaborative efforts to assemble the work of artists from every corner of ASEAN. Many have joined us for this occasion today. They are rising stars, with a bright future in their countries and gaining growing reputations within the region.
A community of artists is emerging, with few opportunities to display their works alongside those of their regional counterparts. Our exhibition will, we hope, provides that opportunity and fosters that cross-border cooperation that is integral to the development of art in a dynamic community.
Even though this process might be organic, there are increasing initiatives within ASEAN to cement these artistic relationships.
Many ASEAN initiatives have expanded the tourism industry significantly over the last few years. This should prove useful as tourists cum roving art lovers can stimulate the art market as history had shown in locations such as Renaissance Italy or in modern Bali. I envisage innovation such as the GOASEAN travel channel would further promote the region as a tourist destination and would further propel understandings on the heritage and culture among the ASEAN member countries.
Common understanding and closeness cannot be forced by decree. It needs the ambassadorial skills of the artist, an individual who can usually see that one person's gain is not another's loss. What they really want is an audience, preferably with customers included. As the economies of ASEAN countries strengthen and societies become wealthier so does a common sense of purpose and an expanded interest in aesthetic expression.
All ten nations have varied creative aptitudes, just as they have different economic strengths. In both cases, these are greater than the sum of their parts. The challenge is getting to see examples of this diversity side by side. With Our Exhibition, we not only have '
Our
People,
Our Community
,
Our
Vision' but also Our Art Space.
We are doing our small bit, to support the declared ASEAN commitment to community building by dedicating a space to showcase ASEAN works. At all times we have a display of ASEAN paintings in our South Gallery to promote fraternity among the ten nations. This has now been extended to the North Gallery for three months and we look forward to a continuous collaboration stretching into the future.
I would like to thank the artists, galleries and institutions that helped bring these components together. The first of the eight priorities listed at the ASEAN summit is "to formally establish an ASEAN community". With greater cooperation and by leveraging on our different strengths, we can be part of a community that is not only better in terms of prosperity and stability but looks better as well.
Thank you very much and I wish everyone an enjoyable experience of the exhibition.
title: Deputy Governor's Speech at the Launch of "Art of ASEAN: Our Exhibition"

Deputy Governor’s Opening Remarks at the FOMCA Financial Education Conference: "Strengthening Financial Resilience of Malaysian Consumers"
Speaker
: Muhammad bin Ibrahim, FCB
Venue
: Sasana Kijang
Delivery Date
:
26 Nov. 2015
It is my pleasure to speak at the Conference on Strengthening Financial Resilience of Malaysian Consumers this morning. It is important for all consumers to be equipped with financial knowledge and skills, in order to reap the benefits of economic growth and be resilient against changes in financial circumstances. Bank Negara Malaysia (the Bank) is pleased to have been collaborating with the Federation of Malaysian Consumers Association (FOMCA) and its associates for many years to elevate the financial capability of Malaysian consumers. This Conference by FOMCA and Education and Research Association for Consumers, Malaysia (ERA) represents another opportunity for the public and private sectors in Malaysia tocome together to further advance the financial literacy agenda. I would also like to record our appreciation to CITI Foundation for their support. Collaborative effort is important to promote the financial wellbeing of our society and the soundness and stability of the financial system.
Being financially literate is a critical first step to help Malaysians better cope with changing demographics, rising costs of living, lifestyle pressures and evolving norms. Consumers with financial literacy are able to achieve key financial goals throughout their life stages, such as:
- to accumulate assets and wealth, to start or expand business ventures, to raise a family or to invest for the future; and
- able to create opportunities to improve standards of living across the board, despite individual circumstances.
We are living in challenging times. A key concern in the current environment is to enhance the skills and capability of financial consumers, in particular households and small businesses, to manage competing demands on their limited resources. We must equip our public with the ability to manage their debt and expenditures wisely, and making saving and investment decisions in an increasingly complex financial environment.
Efforts to enhance the financial competence of consumers have evolved over a span of two decades in this country. Consumers are becoming more knowledgeable and have greater confidence to make informed decisions on an expanding range of financial products, services and delivery channels. Despite this, financial capability among Malaysian consumers still remains relatively behind in comparison to other advanced economies. This has constrained the benefits that can be gained by consumers from participating in the financial system. Many consumers also continue to fall prey to unscrupulous market practices, in some cases, with severe financial consequences for the victims.
Financial capability therefore is an important life skill. Just like any other life skill, it puts practical knowledge and tools in the hands of individuals that can be used to manage their financial affairs effectively and responsibly. The aim is to create generations of financial consumers who have a realistic grasp of their financial circumstances and can make sound financial choices that will enable them to enjoy a comfortable life. This is possible by nurturing prudent financial management traits such as:
The ability to live within one’s means;
Understanding the benefits, risks and costs before purchasing a financial product;
Able to differentiate and deal only with licensed and legitimate financial institutions;
Knowing how and where to seek help early when experiencing financial distress; and
Taking concrete steps to save and invest for the future.
These traits continue to represent the central themes in the Bank’s financial education strategies.
To be effective, financial education policies and strategies should ideally be supported by concrete evidence to ensure better use of resources and ensure that the financial education strategies are designed to address the specific needs of consumers. The use of strong evidence ensures that the nature and the extent of the problems are well understood, and the choice and design of the policy intervention to deal with the problem is optimal. This is particularly important for financial education programmes given that the programmes are very resource and time intensive, thus requiring such significant investments are properly accounted and justified.
The recent nationwide Financial Capability and Inclusion Demand Side Survey 2015 conducted by the Bank has provided some useful insights on the key vulnerabilities and gaps faced by Malaysian households. This will be shared in more detail during the morning panel session today. In summary, the study reveals that while the financial infrastructure to promote access and utilisation of financial products and services are well developed in Malaysia but consumers generally lack the capability to make good financial decisions and do not have sufficient means to effectively participate in the financial system.
This has important implications for financial education policies and strategies. One implication is that for the vulnerable segments of the population, the financial capability strategies need to be accompanied by concrete measures for income generation. The study highlights the inability of the lower income group to effectively participate in the financial system due to limited financial resources. Whatever resources they possess are predominantly utilised to meet essential needs with no financial buffers for the future.
Another important implication is the need to better understand behaviour in financial decision making as a stronger basis for developing more effective financial education strategies. The application of such behavioural insights has substantial potential for improving financial decisions by consumers. It can provide insights on the way information ought to be presented to make it more intuitive to consumers, and focus our thinking on the appropriate design of financial education programmes so that they become more relevant and create a more lasting impact on financial behaviour. It is therefore important that greater collaboration to understand behavioural finance among key stakeholders and identify the levers that contribute to better financial decisions by consumers in different circumstances.
It is also important to ensure that financial education initiatives are sustainable in promoting positive financial behaviours over time. Since 2011,financial education programmes in Malaysia have been designed and delivered to equip Malaysians of all ages with knowledge on financial management which are relevant to their stage in life. Among young Malaysian, focus is directed at inculcating good financial management habits that will positively shape their attitude towards financial matters.
We are collaborating with the Ministry of Education (MOE) in designing a systematic integration of key elements of financial education curriculum for primary and secondary schools beginning 2014 and2017 respectively. We envisage that this will be extended to all school levels by 2021. This is a major breakthrough. We are laying the foundation for developing a financially capable society. In parallel, financial education programmes that target adults are being driven by Agensi Kaunseling Dan Pengurusan Kredit (or AKPK), alongside its debt management programmes. It is a comprehensive approach in providing support for Malaysians in managing their personal finances.
In our work on financial education, the Bank has constantly strived to ensure that we are connecting with consumers in ways that are relevant to the times. In 2003, we published information booklets that educated the public on financial products and services. As internet usage increased, we also developed the
bankinginfo
and
insuranceinfo
websites, alongside online financial tools. BNM Telelink was introduced in 2007 to facilitate prompt and efficient response to issues or queries received from the public via telephone, fax, letter or email on matters related to the financial sector. BNM MobileLINK, introduced in 2011, provides an innovative channel for consumers in semi-urban and non-urban areas to interface with the Bank. Today, we continue to convey important messages to financial consumers through diverse channels including print media, radio, news portals and social media. The use of technology, in particular, to empower consumers with the appropriate information to aid in decision-making has been a central part of the innovation that we have been able to achieve in the area of financial education.In this context, mobile devices have become important tools that can also be leveraged on to support effective financial decision-making.
In carrying this work forward, we are pleased to introduce today three new mobile applications that will help consumers make better financial decisions.
These applications build on smart phone technology. Research has found that smart phones can have a significant impact in helping consumers make smarter choices. Study revealed that 70% of users who browse product reviews or get product information while shopping actually change their purchase decision. We shall use this insight. We are introducing three mobile applications:
MyBNM,
whichallowsconsumers to keep abreast with the latest financial news including announcements, financial fraud alerts and foreign exchange rates at their fingertips. The apps would assists consumers who seek information on the latest developments on the financial industry as well as updates on monetary and financial policies and regulations by the Bank.
BNM MyLINK
- is a one-stop mobile application which provides a direct interface between consumers and financial service providers in Malaysia. It provides a directory of conventional and Islamic banking, insurance and takaful companies as well as SME institutions which allow consumers to connect directly with financial service providers to make enquiries, obtain advice and address their complaints.
MyTabung
-is a tool for individuals to create a personal or household budget. Users can capture incomes, savings and recurring expenses with an on-the-spot display of the user’s financial standing and spending patterns. Individuals can also obtain financial advice and budgeting tips to guide them in practicing prudent financial management as a way of life.
These mobile applications are available in both Bahasa Malaysia and English, and can be downloaded for free from Apple App Store and Google Play Store.
We would like to invite all of you to visit our booth outside this Conference Hall to learn more about the mobile applications. The Bank had also earlier in May 2015 launched a mobile application named MyRinggit which helps consumers identify the security features of the Malaysian currency.
Greater public and private sector collaboration toaddress the needs of consumers for reliable and professional financial advice must also be encouraged. Given the multiple facets of financial education content and programmes, there is an opportunity for the various key stakeholders to come together to align strategies, reduce duplication and identify gaps in order to maximise our collective impact while using resources in the most efficient way. It has been the Bank’s observation that coordinated financial education strategies tend to be sustained longer as there is greater focus, more optimal resource allocation and a more visible impact. In Malaysia, the Bank coordinates closely with various organisations including AKPK, the Securities Commission, Perbadanan Insurans Deposit Malaysia, Kumpulan Wang Simpanan Pekerja and consumer associations on financial education initiatives. Existing informal arrangements have the potential to be further expanded and developed to provide a national platform for articulating and driving a clear national financial education agenda and strategy for Malaysia.
Strengthening the financial resilience of Malaysian is not just about educating them to make better financial choices, but is also about providing our consumers with the means to manage the effects of those choices, especially where consumers are disadvantaged in terms of relative power compared to the financial institutions that they deal with. Therefore, it has always been a priority of the Bank to develop a robust and effective advisory and redress mechanisms. This mechanism is an important part of the consumer protection and empowerment framework in Malaysia.
The Bank, through BNMLINK and BNMTELELINK has advised close to 3 million financial consumers on financial matters or disputes with financial service providers. The establishment of a Financial Ombudsman Scheme (FOS) in early 2016 will further strengthen the financial dispute resolution arrangements available for consumers. The scheme will provide financial consumers with an effective and independent redress mechanism with minimum formality to resolve disputes between consumers and financial services providers. The service offered will be an alternative to the courts. In addition, AKPK will continue to provide financial education, credit counselling and debt management services at no cost to consumers.
Conclusion
The role of financial education has become even more important as a means to strengthen the financial resilience of consumers in a dynamic and constantly changing environment. More importantly, it needs to be approached holistically together with the consumer protection and financial inclusion agenda to achieve a lasting impact on improving the financial well-being of society. We have a pressing need for better research to enable us to design an effective financial education intervention policy and to prioritise where resources can be best allocated. From the national perspective, we need to better coordinate our efforts to leverage on available resources and generate innovative ideas to improve the effectiveness in delivering financial education to diverse audiences with multiple needs. It is my hope that deliberations at this Conference will lead to pragmatic and concrete steps that we can take collectively to elevate the level of financial capability and resilience for all Malaysians.
On this note, I now declare open this conference, wish all of you an engaging and productive Conference.
title: Deputy Governor’s Opening Remarks at the FOMCA Financial Education Conference: "Strengthening Financial Resilience of Malaysian Consumers"
